One of the Chrises ruefully admits, 'It's easy for people to forget who they are sometimes.' Perhaps this is true, but in Eno's lovely and thought-provoking play, 'The Underlying Chris' makes a memorable and indelible impression.

Will Eno has gone and changed the math in his witty new work, The Underlying Chris.
It would be easy to make the claim that Will Eno’s exploration of the interconnectedness of life is more confusing than complex.
But I suspect I’ll likely forget most of the play – if not the extraordinary effort by its players – by the end of 2019.

The underlying problem of The Underlying Chris, however, is that Chris’s life is not a particularly unusual one and, apart from the charm or humor of this or that moment in its enactment, not even a clever gimmick can compel continued interest in it.

cn.t: Will Eno's philosophical meditation on identity follows one character from birth to death, played by eleven diverse actors across twelve life stages. Critics praise its emotional depth, theatrical inventiveness, and accessible exploration of what it means to be human.
